business-model.title: Business Model
business-model.short: How the company creates, delivers and captures value.
business-model.what: A description of what the company sells, to whom, how it delivers it, and how it gets paid. If you can’t explain it in two sentences, you don’t understand it yet.
example: Hard to switch once books are in it
business-model.interp: The business model determines margins, capital needs, cyclicality and how durable revenue is.
compare: How the model has changed over time
business-model.watch: Management’s description can be marketing. Check it against where the revenue and profit actually come from (segment data).

revenue-model.title: Revenue Model
revenue-model.short: How the company charges: one-off, recurring, usage, transaction, advertising…
revenue-model.what: The mechanism by which the company earns revenue: one-time sales, recurring subscriptions, usage-based fees, transaction take-rates, advertising, licensing, hardware + services.
revenue-model.interp: Recurring and contractual revenue is more predictable and usually valued at higher multiples than one-off or project revenue.
better: More recurring revenue is generally higher quality.
compare: Share of recurring vs one-off revenue over time
revenue-model.watch: “Recurring” is sometimes stretched to cover repeat-but-uncontracted purchases.

segments.title: Business Segments
segments.short: The separate units management reports results for.
segments.what: The distinct parts of the company that management reports separately (by product line or geography), each with its own revenue and usually operating profit.
segments.interp: Segments often have very different growth, margins and risk. A great segment can be hidden inside a mediocre consolidated number — or vice versa.
compare: Each segment’s growth and margin trend
segments.watch: Corporate costs are often not allocated to segments, so segment profits add up to more than total operating income.

revenue-mix.title: Revenue Mix
revenue-mix.short: Breakdown of revenue by product, customer, geography or type.
revenue-mix.what: How total revenue splits across products, segments, geographies, customer types, or recurring vs one-off.
revenue-mix.interp: A shift in mix toward higher-margin products raises overall margins even if nothing else changes (“mix shift”).
better: Mix toward faster-growing, higher-margin revenue is usually positive.
revenue-mix.watch: Margin improvement from mix shift is not the same as improvement in each business.

growth-drivers.title: Growth Drivers
growth-drivers.short: What can increase revenue: volume, price, new products, new markets, M&A.
growth-drivers.what: The specific levers that can grow revenue: market expansion, price increases, customer growth, more spend per customer, new products, geographic expansion, acquisitions.
growth-drivers.he: צמיחה = יותר לקוחות × יותר רכישות ללקוח × מחיר גבוה יותר.
growth-drivers.formula:
Revenue = Customers × Revenue per Customer
(or Units × Price)
growth-drivers.interp: Good analysis names the one or two drivers that matter most and checks the evidence for each.
growth-drivers.watch: Growth bought via acquisitions or driven by price alone can fade; organic volume growth is usually higher quality.

competitive-advantage.title: Competitive Advantage
competitive-advantage.short: Why customers choose this company over alternatives.
competitive-advantage.what: Anything that lets a company win customers or earn better economics than competitors: better product, lower cost, brand, distribution, technology.
competitive-advantage.interp: A competitive advantage becomes a moat only when it is durable — hard for competitors to copy for many years.
competitive-advantage.watch: A temporary lead (a hot product) is not the same as a durable structural advantage.

moat.title: Economic Moat
moat.short: A durable structural advantage that protects profits from competitors.
moat.what: A durable structural advantage that protects a company’s profits and returns on capital from competition over many years — like a moat protecting a castle.
moat.he: חפיר כלכלי = יתרון מבני ועמיד שמקשה על מתחרים לגזול את הרווחים.
moat.interp: The financial evidence of a moat is high ROIC sustained for many years, stable or rising margins, and pricing power.
better: Wider and more durable is better.
moat.watch: “No competition” is NOT automatically a moat. The important question is: WHY is competition difficult? If high profits exist and nothing stops others from copying, competitors will come.
moat.body:
Source of moatWhat it meansTypical examples
Network EffectsEach new user makes the product more valuable for others.Marketplaces, payment networks, social platforms
Switching CostsLeaving is painful, risky or expensive.ERP software, core banking, embedded workflows
Economies of ScaleUnit costs fall with size; small rivals can’t match prices profitably.Warehouse retail, cloud infrastructure, chips
BrandCustomers pay more or choose by default because of trust/status.Luxury goods, beverages, consumer tech
Intellectual PropertyPatents, trade secrets, proprietary technology.Pharma, semiconductor design
Cost AdvantageStructurally lower costs from process, location or resources.Low-cost producers, unique mines
DistributionOwns the channel or shelf; reaches customers cheaper.Consumer staples, app stores
Vertical IntegrationControls key parts of the value chain → cost, speed, quality.EVs, aerospace, fashion
Regulatory BarriersLicenses or laws limit who can compete.Utilities, exchanges, defence, rating agencies
Data AdvantageProprietary data improves the product and compounds with usage.Search, credit scoring, mapping

q.tells: Whether today’s high returns are likely to last.
q.compare: ROIC history vs WACC, competitor returns.
q.fool: A temporary product lead, a booming cycle, or a monopoly that regulators may break up.

market-share.title: Market Share
market-share.what: The company’s portion of total sales in its market.
market-share.formula: Market Share = Company Revenue / Total Market Revenue
market-share.interp: Rising share = winning against competitors. Leading share can bring scale advantages.
better: Rising share is usually good; very high share may invite regulation.
market-share.watch: Depends heavily on how you define “the market”. Share can be bought with unprofitable price cuts.

tam.title: TAM
tam.short: Total annual revenue opportunity if the company had 100% share.
tam.what: The total annual revenue available for a product if the company captured the entire market. Related: SAM (serviceable) and SOM (realistically obtainable).
tam.interp: TAM sets the ceiling on long-term growth. A small company in a big, growing TAM has a long runway.
better: A larger, growing TAM gives a longer runway.
tam.watch: Company-presented TAMs are often hugely inflated. Build your own bottom-up estimate.

competition.title: Competition
competition.short: Who else serves these customers, and how intensely they fight.
competition.what: The other companies (and substitutes) competing for the same customers, and how they compete: price, product, distribution, brand.
competition.interp: Intense competition pushes margins and returns down toward the cost of capital unless a moat protects the company.
competition.watch: New entrants and substitutes from other industries are often missed.

customer-concentration.title: Customer Concentration
customer-concentration.short: How dependent revenue is on a few large customers.
customer-concentration.what: The share of revenue coming from the largest customers. Companies must disclose customers above 10% of revenue.
customer-concentration.interp: High concentration gives big customers bargaining power and creates a cliff risk if one leaves.
customer-concentration.watch: Concentration can rise quietly as a big customer grows faster than others.

cyclicality.title: Cyclicality
cyclicality.short: How much results swing with the economic or industry cycle.
cyclicality.what: The tendency of revenue and profits to rise and fall with the economy or an industry cycle (commodities, autos, semiconductors, housing, airlines).
cyclicality.interp: For cyclicals, today’s earnings may be at a peak or trough — so valuation on current earnings can mislead.
compare: Results across a full cycle (10+ years)
cyclicality.watch: Cyclicals often look cheapest (low P/E) at the peak and most expensive at the bottom.

catalysts.title: Catalysts
catalysts.short: Events that could make the market recognise the value.
catalysts.what: Specific, ideally dated, events that could change how the market sees the company: earnings, product launches, margin inflection, spin-offs, buybacks, regulatory decisions, index inclusion.
catalysts.interp: Without a catalyst, an undervalued stock can stay undervalued for a long time. That delay alone is not a value trap; investigate whether lasting economic damage undermines the valuation.
catalysts.watch: Catalysts that everyone already knows about are usually priced in.

risk-factors.title: Risk Factors
risk-factors.short: What could go wrong — competition, disruption, regulation, debt, dilution…
risk-factors.what: The main things that could hurt the business or the stock: competition, technology disruption, regulation, debt, customer concentration, margin compression, dilution, cyclicality, execution risk.
risk-factors.interp: The 10-K Risk Factors list is long and legalistic; your job is to pick the 3–5 that actually matter and how likely/severe they are.
compare: Last year’s risk factors (new additions are a signal)
risk-factors.watch: The risk that sinks a company is often not on the list — think about what could disrupt the model.

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.short: Total money from selling products/services, before any expenses.
revenue.what: The total amount a company earns from selling its products or services during a period, before any expenses are subtracted. The first line of the income statement — the “top line”.
revenue.he: הכנסות = סך המכירות לפני כל הוצאה.
revenue.formula: Revenue Growth = (Current Revenue − Previous Revenue) / Previous Revenue
revenue.interp: YoY (Year over Year) compares a period with the same period a year earlier (Q2 2026 vs Q2 2025) — removes seasonality. QoQ (Quarter over Quarter) compares with the immediately preceding quarter (Q2 vs Q1) — shows momentum but is distorted by seasonality.
better: Faster growth is usually better — if it is profitable and not bought at any cost.
revenue.watch: Revenue ≠ Profit. Growth can be inflated by acquisitions, currency moves, price-only increases, or one-off contracts. High growth with deep losses can destroy value.
revenue.where: First line of the income statement.

q.tells: Size of the business and pace of demand.
q.hl: Higher growth usually better — if profitable.
q.compare: History, peers, market growth; organic vs acquired.
q.fool: Acquisitions, currency, easy comparisons after a bad year, aggressive revenue recognition.

cogs.title: Cost of Revenue
cogs.short: Direct costs of producing/delivering what was sold.
cogs.what: The direct costs associated with generating revenue — costs that rise and fall with each unit sold. “COGS” is used for physical goods; “Cost of Revenue” is the broader term that also covers services.
example: Raw materials, factory labour, factory overhead, depreciation of production equipment
Cloud hosting, customer support, third-party licences, payment processing
Purchase cost of the merchandise sold, inbound freight, shrinkage
cogs.interp: Revenue − Cost of Revenue = Gross Profit. The lower COGS is relative to revenue, the more each sale contributes to everything else.
better: Lower as a % of revenue (holding quality constant).
cogs.watch: Companies classify costs differently (e.g. shipping, support), which makes peer comparisons tricky.

gross-profit.title: Gross Profit
gross-profit.what: What remains from revenue after paying the direct costs of producing the product or service. It is the pool of money that must pay for R&D, sales, administration, interest, taxes — and profit.
gross-profit.formula: Gross Profit = Revenue − Cost of Revenue
gross-profit.interp: Gross profit should grow at least as fast as revenue. If it grows slower, direct costs are rising faster than prices.
compare: Growth of gross profit vs growth of revenue
gross-profit.watch: A big gross profit does not mean the company is profitable — operating expenses can consume all of it.
gross-profit.where: Often shown directly; otherwise Revenue − Cost of Revenue.

opex.title: Operating Expenses
opex.short: R&D + S&M + G&A — costs of running and growing the company.
opex.what:
Costs of running and growing the business that are not directly tied to each unit sold:
R&D — Research & Development: engineers, new products, technology.
S&M — Sales & Marketing: salespeople, advertising, commissions, customer acquisition.
G&A — General & Administrative: executives, finance, legal, HR, offices.
(S&M + G&A are often reported together as SG&A.)
opex.he: הוצאות תפעול: מו"פ, שיווק ומכירות, הנהלה וכלליות.
opex.formula: Operating Income = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses
opex.interp: Cost of Revenue vs OpEx: Cost of Revenue scales with each unit sold (direct). OpEx is the cost of the organisation — it can grow slower than revenue, which creates operating leverage.
better: Lower as % of revenue is more efficient, but R&D and S&M are also investment in growth.
compare: Each line as % of revenue over time
opex.watch: DO NOT subtract Cost of Revenue twice. Gross Profit already has Cost of Revenue removed. Some data sites show “Total operating expenses” that includes COGS — check before using it.
opex.where: Lines between Gross Profit and Operating Income.

operating-income.title: Operating Income
operating-income.short: Gross Profit − Operating Expenses: profit from core operations.
operating-income.what: Profit from the company’s core business after all operating costs, before interest and taxes. It measures how profitable the operations are, regardless of how the company is financed.
operating-income.he: רווח תפעולי — הרווח מפעילות הליבה, לפני ריבית ומסים.
operating-income.formula: Operating Income = Gross Profit − Operating Expenses
operating-income.interp: Strictly, EBIT (Earnings Before Interest and Taxes) also includes non-operating income; in practice the two are often used interchangeably.
operating-income.watch: One-off items (restructuring, impairments, legal settlements) can distort it. Check “adjusted” figures against GAAP.

net-income.title: Net Income
net-income.short: Profit left for shareholders after all expenses, interest and taxes.
net-income.what: What remains after operating expenses, interest, taxes, and other income/expenses. The “bottom line”, attributable to shareholders.
net-income.he: רווח נקי — הרווח החשבונאי שנשאר לבעלי המניות.
net-income.formula: Net Income = Operating Income − Interest ± Other Income/Expenses − Taxes
net-income.interp: Net income is accounting profit, not cash. It includes non-cash items (depreciation, stock-based compensation) and timing differences (receivables).
net-income.watch: One-off gains (selling a business, investment gains, tax benefits) can inflate it. Profit ≠ Cash Flow.
net-income.where: Last main line of the income statement.

gross-margin.title: Gross Margin
gross-margin.short: Gross Profit / Revenue — what is left after direct costs.
gross-margin.what: Gross Margin shows how much of a company’s revenue remains after paying the direct costs required to produce its products or services.
gross-margin.he: מתוך כל 100$ מכירות — כמה נשאר אחרי העלות הישירה?
gross-margin.interp: For every $100 in revenue, the company retains $60 after direct production/service costs. High gross margin often signals pricing power or a differentiated product.
better: But margins must be compared within the same industry.
gross-margin.watch: Different industries naturally have very different Gross Margins. A supermarket (~25%) and a software company (~75%) should not be compared directly.

q.fool: Industry differences, cost classification choices, mix shifts.

operating-margin.title: Operating Margin
operating-margin.short: Operating Income / Revenue — profit from core operations per $ of sales.
operating-margin.what: The share of revenue left as operating profit after all operating costs — direct costs and R&D, sales and administration.
operating-margin.interp: Gross vs Operating margin: gross margin shows product economics; operating margin shows the economics of the whole company. A company can have high gross margin but low or negative operating margin if it invests heavily in R&D, sales or infrastructure.
better: Unless it is depressed deliberately by growth investment.
operating-margin.watch: Gross Margin ≠ Operating Margin. One-off charges, capitalised costs, or excluding stock-based compensation (“adjusted”) can flatter it.

q.tells: Profitability of the core business after all operating costs.
q.fool: Growth spending, one-offs, “adjusted” numbers excluding real costs.

operating-leverage.title: Operating Leverage
operating-leverage.short: When revenue grows faster than costs, margins expand.
operating-leverage.what: The effect of fixed costs: when a large part of costs is fixed, revenue growth produces proportionally larger growth in operating income — margins expand. It also works in reverse when revenue falls.
operating-leverage.interp: Revenue grew 20% but operating income more than doubled. This is why investors tolerate low margins in scaling businesses. Negative operating leverage occurs when operating expenses grow faster than revenue and squeeze Operating Margin, other things equal. Check Gross Margin as well: revenue outgrowing operating expenses alone does not guarantee better margins.
better: Great on the way up, painful on the way down.
operating-leverage.watch: Expected operating leverage often fails to appear if the company keeps raising spending.
operating-leverage.where: Observed over several years of income statements.
operating-leverage.body:

  2. Operating Expenses ↑ more slowly
  3. Operating Margin ↑ (assuming stable Gross Margin)

net-margin.title: Net Profit Margin
net-margin.short: Net Income / Revenue — bottom-line profit per $ of sales.
net-margin.what: The share of revenue that ends up as net income for shareholders.
net-margin.interp: The company keeps $5 of net profit for every $100 of revenue.
compare: Operating margin (gap shows interest and taxes)
net-margin.watch: Affected by interest, taxes, one-off gains and losses — less “pure” than operating margin.

q.tells: How much of each sale becomes accounting profit for owners.
q.fool: One-offs, tax benefits, investment gains, high leverage.

profit-vs-cash.title: PROFIT ≠ CASH
profit-vs-cash.short: Why net income and cash generated differ.
profit-vs-cash.what: Net income follows accrual accounting: revenue is recorded when earned and costs when incurred — not when cash moves. So a profitable company can have weak cash flow (customers haven’t paid, inventory piling up, heavy CapEx), and a company can temporarily generate cash despite weak earnings (customers prepay, suppliers paid later, large non-cash charges).
profit-vs-cash.he: רווח חשבונאי אינו מזומן. חברה רווחית יכולה להיתקע בלי מזומנים.
profit-vs-cash.body:
ItemBeginner explanationCash vs profit
DepreciationAn old equipment purchase is expensed gradually over its life. The expense reduces profit, but no cash leaves today (it left when the asset was bought).Cash > Profit
Accounts ReceivableYou sold on credit: revenue and profit are booked, but the customer hasn’t paid yet.Cash < Profit
Accounts PayableYou received goods but haven’t paid the supplier yet — the cost is booked, cash is still in the bank.Cash > Profit
Working CapitalThe cash tied up in day-to-day operations (inventory + receivables − payables). When it grows, it absorbs cash.Either way
Stock-Based CompensationEmployees paid in shares: an expense with no cash out — but it dilutes shareholders. It is a real cost.Cash > Profit
CapExBuying equipment is cash out today, but only reaches the income statement slowly as depreciation.Cash < Profit
profit-vs-cash.interp: Over many years, good businesses convert most of their net income into free cash flow. Persistent gaps need an explanation.
compare: Net Income vs Operating Cash Flow over 3–5 years
profit-vs-cash.watch: Net income consistently above operating cash flow can signal aggressive accounting (receivables growing faster than sales). FCF that ignores SBC overstates owner cash.
profit-vs-cash.where: Reconciliation at the top of the Cash Flow Statement.

working-capital.title: Working Capital
working-capital.short: Current assets − current liabilities; cash tied up in daily operations.
working-capital.what: The money tied up in running the business day to day. Accounting definition: current assets − current liabilities. Operating version: receivables + inventory − payables.
working-capital.formula: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
working-capital.interp: An increase in working capital uses cash (reduces operating cash flow); a decrease releases cash.
better: Lower working-capital needs per $ of revenue = more cash-efficient growth.
compare: Working capital as % of revenue over time
working-capital.watch: One-time working-capital releases can make a single year’s cash flow look unusually strong.

cfs.title: Cash Flow Statement
cfs.short: Operating, Investing and Financing cash flows.
cfs.what: Shows the actual cash coming in and going out, split into three sections:
cfs.body:
Operating Cash Flow (OCF)

Cash from normal business operations.

  • Cash collected from customers
  • Paid to suppliers & employees
  • Interest & taxes paid
Investing Cash Flow

Spending on (or selling) long-term assets.

  • CapEx: factories, servers, equipment
  • Acquisitions
  • Buying/selling investments
Financing Cash Flow

Cash to/from owners and lenders.

  • Borrowing / repaying debt
  • Issuing shares
  • Buybacks
  • Dividends
cfs.interp: A healthy mature company: strongly positive OCF, negative investing (reinvesting), negative financing (returning cash / repaying debt).
cfs.watch: Positive financing cash flow every year means the company depends on outside money.

ocf.title: Operating Cash Flow
ocf.short: Cash generated by normal business operations.
ocf.what: The cash a company generates from its normal operations during a period. It starts from net income, adds back non-cash expenses (depreciation, SBC), and adjusts for working-capital changes.
ocf.formula: OCF ≈ Net Income + Depreciation & Amortization + SBC ± Change in Working Capital
ocf.interp: Strong, growing OCF (above net income) suggests high-quality earnings and a business that funds itself.
compare: Net Income (OCF/NI > 1 is a good sign)
ocf.watch: OCF can be boosted temporarily by delaying supplier payments or selling receivables. SBC is added back even though it dilutes owners.
ocf.where: “Net cash provided by operating activities” in the Cash Flow Statement.

capex.title: CapEx
capex.short: Cash spent on long-term physical assets.
capex.what:
Cash spent buying or upgrading long-lived assets: factories, servers, data centres, machinery, vehicles, infrastructure.
Maintenance CapEx — needed just to keep the existing business running (replacing worn-out assets).
Growth CapEx — spending to expand capacity and future revenue.
capex.he: השקעות הוניות: תחזוקה (לשמור על הקיים) מול צמיחה (להתרחב).
example: Remaining spending, if attributable to growth
capex.interp: Growth investment can reduce current FCF below a no-growth cash-generation estimate. Do not remove that spending while retaining the future growth it supports.
better: High CapEx is NOT automatically bad — what matters is the return it earns.
compare: Asset age, replacement costs, and depreciation assumptions
capex.watch: High CapEx is not automatically bad — the company may be investing in future growth. The maintenance/growth split is often an estimate. Depreciation allocates historical costs; inflation, technology changes, and deferred upkeep can make it a poor estimate of required maintenance.
capex.where: Investing section of the Cash Flow Statement (shown as a negative number).

fcf.title: Free Cash Flow
fcf.short: Operating Cash Flow − CapEx: cash left after investment.
fcf.what: The cash generated after paying for the investment needed to maintain and grow the business — the cash truly available to owners.
fcf.he: תזרים מזומנים חופשי = מזומן מפעילות פחות השקעות הוניות.
fcf.interp: Investors care because FCF is what a company can use to: reinvest, pay debt, buy back shares, pay dividends, acquire companies, or hold cash. A business is ultimately worth the FCF it will generate (see DCF).
better: Read it together with growth investment.
fcf.watch: FCF ignores stock-based compensation (a real cost). Cutting CapEx raises FCF short term but may hurt growth. FCF must be understood in the context of growth investment.
fcf.where: Calculated from the Cash Flow Statement.

q.tells: Real cash the business produces for owners.
q.fool: SBC, working-capital swings, temporarily cut CapEx.

fcf-margin.title: FCF Margin
fcf-margin.short: FCF / Revenue — cash generated per $ of sales.
fcf-margin.what: Free cash flow as a percentage of revenue.
fcf-margin.interp: For every $100 of sales, $12 becomes free cash. Compare with operating margin: much lower FCF margin → heavy CapEx or working capital; higher → strong cash conversion (e.g. customer prepayments).
fcf-margin.watch: Lumpy CapEx or working capital can distort a single year — look at multi-year averages.
fcf-margin.where: Calculated: Cash Flow Statement + Income Statement.

assets.title: Assets
assets.short: Resources the company owns/controls that provide future benefit.
assets.what: Everything the company owns or controls that is expected to bring future economic benefit. Split into current (turn into cash within ~1 year) and long-term.
assets.body:
Current AssetsCash, accounts receivable, inventory, short-term investments
Long-Term AssetsPP&E, goodwill & intangibles, long-term investments, lease assets
compare: Asset growth vs revenue growth (asset efficiency)
assets.watch: Assets are mostly recorded at historical cost, not current value. Goodwill can be large and later written down.
assets.where: Top half (or left side) of the Balance Sheet.

current-assets.title: Current Assets
current-assets.short: Assets expected to turn into cash within a year.
current-assets.what: Assets that will be converted to cash or used up within about one year: cash, receivables, inventory, prepaid expenses, short-term investments.
current-assets.watch: Not all current assets are equally liquid — obsolete inventory or doubtful receivables may never become cash.

cash.title: Cash & Cash Equivalents
cash.short: Money in the bank plus very liquid short-term investments.
cash.what: Money in the bank and very liquid, low-risk investments (Treasury bills, money-market funds). Many analysts add short-term investments too.
cash.interp: Why it matters: stability — cash lets a company survive downturns and invest when others can’t. Valuation — cash belongs to shareholders, so it is subtracted in Enterprise Value and added back in the DCF equity bridge.
better: More is safer, but very large idle cash may earn little.
cash.watch: Some cash may be trapped abroad, restricted, or needed for operations (e.g. customer funds held by payment companies).

receivables.title: Accounts Receivable
receivables.short: Money customers owe for things already delivered.
receivables.what: Amounts customers owe for goods/services already delivered but not yet paid for.
receivables.interp: Receivables growing much faster than revenue may signal looser credit terms, collection problems, or aggressive revenue recognition.
better: Lower relative to revenue = faster collection.
receivables.watch: Rising receivables make profit look better than cash.

inventory.title: Inventory
inventory.short: Goods held for sale, in production, or raw materials.
inventory.what: Raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods not yet sold.
inventory.interp: Inventory ties up cash. Rising faster than sales can foreshadow discounts and write-downs.
better: Lower relative to sales = more efficient.
inventory.watch: Obsolete or fashion-sensitive inventory may be worth far less than its book value.

ppe.title: PP&E
ppe.short: Long-term physical assets: buildings, factories, machines, servers.
ppe.what: Physical long-term assets used to operate the business, shown net of accumulated depreciation.
ppe.interp: CapEx increases PP&E; depreciation reduces it. Capital-intensive businesses have large PP&E relative to revenue.
ppe.watch: Recorded at historical cost less depreciation — may differ greatly from replacement or market value.

liabilities.title: Liabilities
liabilities.short: What the company owes to others.
liabilities.what: Obligations the company owes: suppliers, lenders, employees, tax authorities, customers who prepaid. Split into current (due within ~1 year) and long-term.
liabilities.body:
Current LiabilitiesAccounts payable, short-term debt, accrued expenses, deferred revenue
Long-Term LiabilitiesLong-term debt, lease liabilities, pensions, deferred taxes
liabilities.watch: Not all liabilities are bad: deferred revenue is cash customers already paid.
liabilities.where: Bottom half of the Balance Sheet.

current-liabilities.title: Current Liabilities
current-liabilities.what: Obligations due within about a year: accounts payable, short-term debt and current portion of long-term debt, accrued expenses, deferred revenue.
current-liabilities.watch: Large debt maturities inside current liabilities can be a refinancing risk.

payables.title: Accounts Payable
payables.short: Money the company owes its suppliers.
payables.what: Bills from suppliers the company has received but not yet paid.
payables.interp: Paying suppliers later keeps cash longer — a free source of financing for companies with bargaining power.
payables.watch: Stretching payables can boost cash flow temporarily — it can’t continue forever.

debt.title: Debt
debt.short: Money borrowed that must be repaid with interest.
debt.what:
Borrowed money (bank loans, bonds) that must be repaid with interest.
Short-Term Debt — due within a year (including the current portion of long-term debt).
Long-Term Debt — due after more than a year.
debt.interp: Interest burden: interest payments reduce profit and cash. Maturity risk: debt must be repaid or refinanced when due — dangerous if it comes due when credit markets are closed or the business is weak.
better: Less debt = more resilience (though some cheap debt can be efficient).
debt.watch: Leases and other obligations behave like debt but may not be included in “debt” on data sites.
debt.where: Current and long-term liabilities; debt maturity note in the 10-K.

net-cash.title: Net Cash
net-cash.what: Cash minus total debt. If positive, the company has more cash than debt.
net-cash.interp: Positive net cash means the company could repay all its debt today and still have cash left — financial flexibility for downturns, buybacks or acquisitions. Cash > Debt means Net Cash. EV = Market Cap − Net Cash: $20B equity with $3B Net Cash implies $17B EV.
compare: Market Cap (what % of the value is cash?)
net-cash.watch: Some cash may be needed to run the business or be trapped abroad.

net-debt.title: Net Debt
net-debt.what: Total debt minus cash. Used when debt exceeds cash.
net-debt.interp: Analysts care more about net debt than gross debt because cash could be used to repay debt. Two companies each with $10B of debt are very different if one has $9B of cash. Debt > Cash means Net Debt. EV = Market Cap + Net Debt: $20B equity with $8B Net Debt implies $28B EV.
net-debt.watch: Assumes all cash is available to repay debt, which may not be true.

current-ratio.title: Current Ratio
current-ratio.short: Current Assets / Current Liabilities — short-term liquidity.
current-ratio.what: Measures whether short-term assets cover short-term obligations.
current-ratio.formula: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
current-ratio.interp: 2.0 means $2 of current assets for every $1 of current liabilities.
better: Higher = more liquid, but too high can mean idle capital.
current-ratio.watch: Limitations: inventory may not be sellable; receivables may not be collected; subscription companies often run below 1.0 safely because of deferred revenue; it says nothing about long-term debt.

q.hl: Higher is safer, up to a point.
q.fool: Illiquid inventory, deferred revenue, timing of the balance-sheet date.

equity.title: Shareholders’ Equity
equity.short: Assets − Liabilities: the owners’ accounting claim.
equity.what: What would be left for shareholders if all assets were sold at book value and all liabilities paid.
equity.interp: Grows with retained profits and share issuance; shrinks with losses, dividends and buybacks.
equity.watch: Large buybacks can make equity small or even negative in excellent businesses.

book-value.title: Book Value
book-value.short: Accounting value of equity — not market value.
book-value.what: The accounting value of shareholders’ equity on the balance sheet. Per share: Equity / Shares.
book-value.formula:
Book Value = Assets − Liabilities
Price / Book = Market Cap / Book Value
book-value.interp: Book Value ≠ Market Value. Book value reflects historical accounting; market value reflects expectations about future cash flows. Asset-light businesses (software, brands) trade far above book.
book-value.watch: Most useful for banks and asset-heavy firms; nearly meaningless for many tech companies.

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.abbr: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization
ebitda.short: Operating Income + D&A. A rough earnings proxy — not cash.
ebitda.what: Operating profit before deducting depreciation and amortization (and before interest and taxes).
ebitda.he: EBITDA — רווח לפני ריבית, מסים, פחת והפחתות. איננו תזרים מזומנים!
ebitda.interp: Analysts use it to compare businesses with different debt, tax and depreciation policies. Lenders use it to size debt and set covenants (Debt/EBITDA). It is useful for comparing businesses because it is capital-structure neutral.
compare: CapEx (how much EBITDA is really consumed?)
ebitda.watch: EBITDA ≠ CASH FLOW. It ignores CapEx, working capital, interest and taxes. It can make capital-intensive businesses look much better than they are — depreciation reflects equipment that must be replaced.
ebitda.where: Calculated (sometimes reported as “Adjusted EBITDA” — check what’s excluded).

q.tells: Rough operating earnings power before capital structure.
q.hl: Higher is better, but it isn’t cash.
q.fool: Capital intensity, “adjusted” add-backs (SBC, restructuring every year).

debt-ebitda.title: Debt / EBITDA
debt-ebitda.short: Total Debt / EBITDA — rough leverage in “years of EBITDA”.
debt-ebitda.what: A rough measure of leverage: how many years of EBITDA it would take to repay all debt.
debt-ebitda.interp: Conceptually: 1x — debt equals one year of EBITDA, light. 2x — two years. 5x — five years of all EBITDA, heavy for most businesses. There are no universal thresholds: stable utilities carry more debt safely than cyclical or fast-changing businesses.
debt-ebitda.watch: EBITDA ignores CapEx and can collapse in a downturn, so leverage can rise suddenly.
debt-ebitda.where: Calculated from Balance Sheet + Income Statement.

q.tells: How heavy the debt load is relative to earnings power.
q.compare: Peers in the same industry, covenants.

nopat.title: NOPAT
nopat.what: Operating profit after tax, calculated as if the company had no debt. It isolates the profit produced by the operations.
nopat.he: רווח תפעולי אחרי מס — בלי השפעת המימון.
nopat.interp: Why NOPAT instead of Net Income for ROIC? Net income is after interest, so it depends on how much debt the company has. ROIC measures return to all capital (debt + equity), so the numerator must be before interest — NOPAT.
nopat.watch: Use a realistic (effective/cash) tax rate; one-off items in operating income distort it.

invested-capital.title: Invested Capital
invested-capital.short: Capital put into the operating business (Equity + Debt − Cash, simplified).
invested-capital.what: The amount of capital invested in the operating business — the money shareholders and lenders have put in to buy the factories, equipment, inventory and acquisitions the business runs on.
invested-capital.formula: Simple version:  Invested Capital = Shareholders’ Equity + Debt − Cash
invested-capital.interp: There are several detailed ways analysts calculate it — e.g. the operating approach: Net PP&E + Net Working Capital (+ Goodwill & Intangibles). Different methods give different ROICs; be consistent.
better: Less capital needed for the same profit is better.
invested-capital.watch: Goodwill from acquisitions, buybacks (reduce equity), and negative working capital can make it tiny or distorted.

roic.title: ROIC
roic.short: NOPAT / Invested Capital — operating return per $ of capital.
roic.what: Measures how efficiently the business converts invested capital into after-tax operating profit.
roic.he: תשואה על ההון המושקע — כמה רווח מייצר כל דולר שהושקע בעסק.
roic.interp: The business generates approximately $0.20 of after-tax operating profit for every $1 of invested capital. Consistently high ROIC (e.g. 15%+ for many years) is strong evidence of a moat and a high-quality business — competitors would normally compete those returns away.
roic.watch: Accounting differences, acquisitions (goodwill), unusual capital structure, and one-time items can all distort ROIC. One great year proves nothing.
roic.where: Calculated from Income Statement + Balance Sheet.

q.fool: Accounting differences, acquisitions, unusual capital structure, one-time items.

roic.body:
ROIC vs WACC

  • ROIC > WACC — generally creates economic value.
  • ROIC < WACC — may destroy economic value.
  • ROIC ≈ WACC — approximately earns its Cost of Capital.

ROIC − WACC Spread

Value Creation Spread = ROIC − WACC

ROIC 18% − WACC 9% = +9 percentage points. A positive spread is generally desirable.

Check sustainable, forward-looking incremental returns. Historical average ROIC can hide weak new projects.

wacc.title: WACC
wacc.short: The return investors require — the hurdle ROIC must beat.
wacc.what: WACC is the blended required return of the providers financing a business: primarily equity investors and debt investors. It is the typical Discount Rate for FCFF.
wacc.he: WACC — התשואה המינימלית שהמשקיעים דורשים. ROIC גבוה ממנה = יצירת ערך.
wacc.formula: WACC = (Equity Weight × Cost of Equity) + (Debt Weight × Cost of Debt × (1 − Tax Rate))
wacc.interp: Use market-value equity and debt weights that sum to 100%. Interest may reduce taxable income, so the debt cost is adjusted for the usable tax benefit. The adjustment assumes interest deductions can be used.
better: For the company, a lower cost of capital is better; for analysis what matters is the spread.
wacc.watch: WACC is an estimate, not a universal fixed hurdle. Deduction limits or tax losses can reduce the usable tax benefit. Use cost of equity for FCFE. Growth creates value only when incremental returns exceed the appropriate cost of capital.
wacc.body:
1. Future FCFF
  2. Discount using WACC
  3. Present Value of FCFF
  4. Enterprise Value (including discounted Terminal Value)

For positive future cash flows, all else equal: Higher WACC → Lower Enterprise Value; Lower WACC → Higher Enterprise Value.

shares-outstanding.title: Shares Outstanding
shares-outstanding.short: Number of shares currently held by investors.
shares-outstanding.what: The total number of shares currently issued and held by investors (excluding treasury shares the company bought back).
shares-outstanding.interp: Used to convert company-level numbers into per-share numbers (EPS, value per share) and to calculate Market Cap.
better: A falling share count (buybacks) increases each owner’s slice.
shares-outstanding.watch: Use diluted shares for valuation. The cover page of the 10-K/10-Q shows the latest count.
shares-outstanding.where: Bottom of the Income Statement (weighted average) and 10-K cover page.

basic-shares.title: Basic Shares
basic-shares.what: The weighted-average number of shares actually outstanding during the period. Used for Basic EPS.
compare: Diluted shares (the gap shows potential dilution)
basic-shares.watch: Ignores options, RSUs and convertibles that will likely become shares.

diluted-shares.title: Diluted Shares
diluted-shares.short: Basic shares + shares that could be created from options, RSUs, convertibles.
diluted-shares.what: Basic shares plus all shares that could be created from stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), warrants and convertible bonds. Used for Diluted EPS and fair value per share.
diluted-shares.interp: The more conservative and correct denominator for valuation.
diluted-shares.watch: Even “diluted” may understate future dilution if the company keeps granting large stock compensation.

dilution.title: Dilution
dilution.short: Issuing new shares shrinks each existing shareholder’s slice.
dilution.what: When a company issues new shares (to employees via stock compensation, to raise money, or for acquisitions), each existing share owns a smaller percentage of the company.
dilution.formula: Annual dilution = (Shares this year − Shares last year) / Shares last year
dilution.interp: A company can grow while existing shareholders are diluted: the company got bigger, but your slice grew much less.
better: Below ~1–2% per year is modest; buybacks reverse it.
dilution.watch: Companies may offset dilution with buybacks — check how much cash buybacks really consume.

eps.title: EPS
eps.what: Net income divided by the number of shares: the profit attributable to each share. Reported as Basic and Diluted EPS.
eps.interp: Per-share metrics matter because shareholders own shares, not the company. EPS growth is what ultimately drives share price over time.
compare: EPS growth vs net income growth (dilution/buybacks)
eps.watch: Buybacks raise EPS without business improvement; “adjusted EPS” often excludes real costs like SBC.

q.compare: Its own growth, net income growth.

market-cap.title: Market Capitalization
market-cap.what: The market value of the company’s equity — what the stock market currently charges for all of its shares.
market-cap.formula: Market Cap = Share Price × Shares Outstanding
market-cap.interp: Share price by itself tells almost nothing about whether a stock is cheap. A $500 stock with 100M shares ($50B) is “smaller” than a $10 stock with 10B shares ($100B). Market Cap values equity, not the underlying operating business. Compare share counts over time: issuance and buybacks change Market Cap even with an unchanged Share Price.
market-cap.watch: Use current shares outstanding for current Market Cap, not weighted-average diluted EPS shares. Track issuance, buybacks and potential dilution separately. Compare the same date for price and shares.

pe.title: P/E
pe.short: Market Cap / Net Income — $ paid per $1 of earnings.
pe.what: How many dollars investors pay for each dollar of the company’s annual earnings.
pe.formula:
P/E = Market Cap / Net Income
P/E = Share Price / EPS
pe.interp: P/E 20x means investors currently pay ~$20 for every $1 of annual earnings (earnings yield = 1/20 = 5%). Growth and quality matter: a fast-growing, high-ROIC company deserves a higher P/E because its future earnings will be much larger.
better: Lower is cheaper only if earnings quality and growth are equal.
pe.watch: Low P/E ≠ automatically cheap (declining business, peak-cycle earnings, one-off gains). High P/E ≠ automatically expensive (fast growth, temporarily depressed earnings). Meaningless when earnings are negative.

q.tells: What the market pays for current earnings.
q.hl: Lower is cheaper — all else equal (it rarely is).
q.fool: Cyclical peaks, one-offs, buybacks, accounting earnings vs cash.

enterprise-value.title: Enterprise Value
enterprise-value.short: Market Cap + Debt − Cash — value of the operating business.
enterprise-value.what: An approximation of the value of the whole operating business, independent of how it is financed.
enterprise-value.he: שווי פירמה: שווי העסק התפעולי — כולל החוב, בניכוי המזומן.
enterprise-value.interp: Imagine buying the whole company: you pay the market cap, but you also take on its debt (you must repay it → add) and you get its cash (it reduces your real cost → subtract). Market Cap = Equity Value. Enterprise Value = approximate value of the operating enterprise. EV approximates operating business value and helps compare different capital structures. Net Cash can put EV below Market Cap; high Net Debt can put it significantly above Market Cap.
enterprise-value.watch: Market Cap ≠ Enterprise Value. A precise EV also adds preferred stock, minority interests and often leases.

ev-ebitda.title: EV / EBITDA
ev-ebitda.what: Values the whole business relative to its EBITDA.
ev-ebitda.interp: Why pair EV with EBITDA? EBITDA is earned before interest, so it belongs to all capital providers (debt and equity) — matching EV, which also includes debt. Useful for comparing companies with different leverage and in M&A.
better: Lower is cheaper, all else equal.
ev-ebitda.watch: Limitations: EBITDA ignores CapEx, so capital-intensive businesses look cheap. Cross-check with EV/EBIT or Price/FCF. “Adjusted EBITDA” may exclude real costs.

q.tells: Price of the whole business per $ of operating earnings before D&A.
q.fool: High CapEx needs, adjusted EBITDA, cyclical peaks.

price-fcf.title: Price / FCF
price-fcf.what: How many dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual free cash flow.
price-fcf.formula: Price / FCF = Market Cap / Free Cash Flow
price-fcf.interp: Like P/E but based on cash rather than accounting profit. 20x means paying $20 for $1 of annual FCF.
better: Lower is cheaper, all else equal.
price-fcf.watch: One year of FCF can be lumpy (CapEx timing, working capital). SBC isn’t deducted.

fcf-yield.title: FCF Yield
fcf-yield.short: FCF / Market Cap — cash generated per $100 of market value.
fcf-yield.what: Annual free cash flow as a percentage of market value — the cash “yield” you get at today’s price.
fcf-yield.formula: FCF Yield = Free Cash Flow / Market Cap
fcf-yield.interp: For every $100 of market value the company generates ~$10 of FCF per year. Inverse of Price/FCF: 10% yield ⇔ 10x P/FCF; 4% ⇔ 25x.
better: Higher may indicate a cheaper valuation — but growth must be considered.
fcf-yield.watch: A high yield with shrinking FCF is a trap; a low yield can be fine with strong growth.

q.tells: Cash return at today’s price, before growth.
q.fool: Declining FCF, one-off FCF spikes, ignoring SBC.

growth-vs-valuation.title: Growth vs Valuation
growth-vs-valuation.what: The central tradeoff of stock valuation: a stock that gives a lot of cash relative to its price today vs one that gives little today but may grow much larger.
growth-vs-valuation.body:
FCF YieldFCF GrowthFCF per $100 — year 0Year 5Year 10
Company A10%3%$10.00$11.59$13.44
Company B4%25%$4.00$12.21$37.25
growth-vs-valuation.interp: A provides much more cash relative to today’s valuation. B provides less current cash but potentially much higher future cash — if growth continues. B overtakes A in year 5. Neither metric (yield or growth) should be viewed alone; a DCF combines both.
growth-vs-valuation.watch: High expected growth is already priced in; if it disappoints, the low-yield stock can fall a lot.

time-value-money.title: Time Value of Money
time-value-money.short: Money today is worth more than the same amount received in the future, when the required return is positive.
time-value-money.what: Money today is worth more than the same amount received in the future, when the required return is positive.
time-value-money.interp: Today’s money can earn investment returns. Waiting has an opportunity cost; inflation reduces purchasing power, and future cash flows carry risk and uncertainty. DCF translates those future cash flows into today’s value.
time-value-money.watch: Match nominal cash flows with nominal rates and real cash flows with real rates. Do not deduct inflation twice.
example: Not economically equivalent at a positive required return.

dcf-intro.title: DCF
dcf-intro.short: Intrinsic value = present value of future free cash flows.
dcf-intro.what: A valuation method that estimates what a business is worth today by forecasting its future free cash flows and discounting them back to the present.
dcf-intro.formula: Value = Σ FCFₜ / (1 + r)ᵗ  +  Terminal Value / (1 + r)ᴺ
dcf-intro.interp: The output is only as good as the assumptions. Use it to understand what you must believe for the stock to be cheap — and what the current price implies.
dcf-intro.watch: DCF is based on assumptions, not certainty. Small changes in growth, r or g move the value a lot.

present-value.title: Present Value
present-value.what: What a future amount of money is worth today. Money today is worth more than money later because it can be invested, and the future is uncertain.
present-value.formula:
PV = Future Cash Flow / (1 + r)^t
PV = Present Value · r = Discount Rate per period · t = Number of periods
present-value.interp: At a 10% required return, receiving $90.91 today is equivalent to $100 in a year. Present Value converts future money into today’s economic value. Use the calculator below; set Years to 10 to reproduce the $38.55 example.
present-value.watch: The further away the cash flow and the higher r, the less it is worth today.

future-value.title: Future Value
future-value.short: Future Value compounds today’s money forward at an assumed rate of return.
future-value.what: Future Value compounds today’s money forward at an assumed rate of return.
future-value.interp: Compounding asks what today’s money will be worth in the future. Discounting reverses the direction: what is future money worth today?
future-value.watch: The assumed return is not guaranteed. Match the rate and period; these examples use annual compounding without fees or taxes.
future-value.body:
Compounding vs Discounting

CompoundingPresent → Future: What will today’s money be worth?
PV × (1 + r)^t = FV
DiscountingFuture → Present: What is future money worth today?
FV / (1 + r)^t = PV

required-return.title: Required Return
required-return.short: The minimum expected return investors require for time, risk and opportunity cost.
required-return.what: The minimum expected return investors require for time, risk and opportunity cost.
required-return.interp: Higher perceived risk generally increases the required return. Match the required return to the claims and cash flows being valued.
required-return.watch: A required return is a hurdle, not a promised or realized return. An arbitrary target does not establish a company’s WACC.

discount-rate.title: Discount Rate
discount-rate.short: The rate matched to the cash flows being valued.
discount-rate.what: The annual rate used to convert future cash into today’s value. It reflects the time value of money and risk — riskier businesses get higher discount rates. Use WACC for FCFF and the cost of equity for FCFE. The Discount Rate is the required return used to calculate Present Value.
discount-rate.interp: Discount Rate ↑ → Valuation ↓. Discount Rate ↓ → Valuation ↑.
discount-rate.watch: Small changes in the rate can materially change DCF value. Match the rate to cash-flow risk, currency and inflation assumptions.
discount-rate.body:
1. Higher Risk
  2. Higher Required Return
  3. Higher Discount Rate
  4. Lower Present Value

The $100 cash flow did not change. Only the required return changed. Higher rates reduce the Present Value of positive future cash flows; lower rates increase it.

Try both rates in the Present Value calculator

terminal-value.title: Terminal Value
terminal-value.short: FCF next year / (r − g): value of all cash after the forecast.
terminal-value.what: We cannot forecast a company year by year forever, so after the explicit forecast (e.g. 10 years) we assume FCF grows at a modest constant rate g forever and capture all of it in one number.
terminal-value.formula:
Terminal Value = FCF next year / (r − g)

r = Discount Rate · g = Terminal Growth Rate
PV of TV = TV / (1 + r)ᴺ
terminal-value.interp: Terminal value often represents 60–80% of a DCF’s total value, because it covers every year after the forecast — that is why DCFs are so sensitive to r and g.
terminal-value.watch: r must be greater than g — otherwise the formula breaks (division by zero or a negative number). g should not exceed long-run economic growth (~2–4%).

dcf-ev.title: DCF Enterprise Value
dcf-ev.short: PV of forecast FCF + PV of terminal value.
dcf-ev.what: The value of the whole operating business implied by your DCF.
dcf-ev.formula: Enterprise Value = PV of Forecast FCF + PV of Terminal Value
dcf-ev.interp: Discount FCFF, the cash flow available to all capital providers, at WACC to estimate operating enterprise value. Discounting FCFE at the cost of equity instead gives equity value.
dcf-ev.watch: Check what share comes from terminal value.

equity-value.title: Equity Value
equity-value.what: The part of enterprise value that belongs to shareholders, after lenders are repaid and cash is added.
equity-value.formula: Equity Value = Enterprise Value − Debt + Cash
equity-value.interp: Comparable to Market Cap. If your equity value is above the market cap, the stock may be undervalued (according to your assumptions).
equity-value.watch: Include all debt-like items (leases, preferred stock, minority interests) for precision.

fair-value-per-share.title: Fair Value Per Share
fair-value-per-share.what: Your estimate of what one share is worth.
fair-value-per-share.formula:
Fair Value Per Share = Equity Value / Diluted Shares Outstanding
Upside / Downside = Fair Value / Current Price − 1
fair-value-per-share.interp: Compare with the current price — but as a range (bear/base/bull), not one number.
fair-value-per-share.watch: Use diluted shares; false precision ($26.37) is a warning sign.

sensitivity.title: Sensitivity Analysis
sensitivity.short: How fair value changes as key assumptions change.
sensitivity.what: Re-running the DCF across a grid of assumptions (typically discount rate × terminal growth) to see a range of values instead of one magical number.
sensitivity.body:
Discount Rate ↑ → Valuation ↓
Discount Rate ↓ → Valuation ↑
Terminal Growth ↑ → Valuation ↑
Terminal Growth ↓ → Valuation ↓
Bear case

Lower growth, lower margins, higher discount rate, conservative terminal assumptions.

Base case

Most reasonable assumptions.

Bull case

Higher growth, higher margins, operating leverage.
sensitivity.interp: A good investment often has limited downside in the bear case and meaningful upside in base/bull. Also ask in reverse: what assumptions are already priced into the stock?
sensitivity.watch: Valuation should be a range, not a single magical number.

thesis-def.title: Investment Thesis
thesis-def.short: Why the stock is mispriced, why it will change, and what would prove you wrong.
thesis-def.what: A concise argument (a few sentences) explaining what you believe that the market doesn’t, why it matters for value, and what will make the market recognise it.
thesis-def.body:
1Business
2Moat
3Growth Drivers
4Financial Quality
5Capital Efficiency
6Valuation
7Catalysts
8Risks
9Bear Case
10Base Case
11Bull Case
12Thesis Invalidation
thesis-def.interp: A good thesis is specific and falsifiable: “Margins will expand from 10% to 18% as data-centre utilisation rises; the market prices in 12%.”
thesis-def.watch: “Great company” is not a thesis. If you can’t say why the market is wrong, you probably don’t have an edge.

invalidation.title: Thesis Invalidation
invalidation.short: Pre-defined conditions that would prove the thesis wrong.
invalidation.what: 3–10 specific, measurable conditions — written before you invest — that would mean your thesis is broken.
invalidation.interp: When a condition triggers, re-underwrite from scratch: would you buy this stock today at this price?
invalidation.watch: Moving the goalposts after the fact (“it’s only temporary”) is confirmation bias in action.

margin-of-safety.title: Margin of Safety
margin-of-safety.short: The discount from a conservative estimate of intrinsic value.
margin-of-safety.what: A purchase price below conservatively estimated intrinsic value leaves room for some errors in your assumptions. The protection depends on the quality of that estimate.
margin-of-safety.formula: Margin of Safety = (Estimated Value − Price) / Estimated Value
margin-of-safety.interp: A 30% discount to value is different from 30% upside from price. Use a range of values and investigate the downside assumptions.
better: A larger discount helps only when the value estimate remains credible.
margin-of-safety.watch: An optimistic valuation can manufacture an apparent discount. No fixed percentage guarantees protection.
margin-of-safety.where: Your valuation model and the current share price.

owner-earnings.title: Owner Earnings
owner-earnings.short: Estimated earnings available after maintaining the business’s operating capacity.
owner-earnings.what: An estimate of cash earning power after the reinvestment needed to preserve current operations and competitive position. It requires judgment about maintenance spending and working capital.
owner-earnings.formula: Owner Earnings ≈ Net Income + D&A − Maintenance CapEx − Required Increase in Operating Working Capital
owner-earnings.interp: This simplified example assumes no other adjustments. Reconcile unusual gains, losses, and other non-cash items individually. Keep stock-based compensation as an economic cost.
better: Examine sustainable owner earnings per share.
owner-earnings.watch: If you start from operating cash flow, working-capital changes are already included. Do not subtract them twice or exclude investment while retaining the growth it funds.
owner-earnings.where: Financial statements, asset notes, and your maintenance estimates.

maintenance-capex.title: Maintenance CapEx
maintenance-capex.short: Investment needed to preserve operating capacity and competitive position.
maintenance-capex.what: Spending needed to sustain the existing business, including necessary replacements and upgrades. The maintenance/growth split is often an estimate rather than a reported accounting line.
example: Remaining spending, if attributable to growth
maintenance-capex.interp: Build a range from asset age, replacement costs, replacement cycles, capacity, and required upgrades. Compare management’s estimates with spending history.
better: Low spending can reflect efficiency or neglected assets.
maintenance-capex.watch: Depreciation allocates historical costs. Inflation, technology, asset age, and deferred upkeep can make it a poor estimate of current maintenance needs.
maintenance-capex.where: PP&E notes, capital-spending disclosures, operating data, and management commentary.

normalized-earnings.title: Normalized Earnings
normalized-earnings.short: Estimated earnings after unusual items and cycle effects are considered.
normalized-earnings.what: An estimate of repeatable earning power. Remove genuinely unusual gains and costs symmetrically, then consider whether current demand, prices, and margins are sustainable.
normalized-earnings.formula: Adjusted Earnings = Reported Earnings − Unusual Gains + Unusual Costs (all after tax)
example: Genuine one-time closure cost, after tax
normalized-earnings.interp: The arithmetic is a starting point. A cyclical company can still have unusually high adjusted earnings at peak demand.
better: Credible estimates matter more than generous adjustments.
normalized-earnings.watch: Repeated restructuring charges are not automatically exceptional. A historical average can also mislead after structural business changes.
normalized-earnings.where: Income statement, footnotes, and financial history.

capital-allocation.title: Capital Allocation
capital-allocation.short: How management deploys cash and financing to build per-share value.
capital-allocation.what: Management chooses between reinvestment, acquisitions, debt repayment, dividends, buybacks, and retaining cash. Judge the results relative to risk and available alternatives.
example: Repurchase shares below conservatively estimated value
capital-allocation.interp: Compare the likely value created by each use of funds. A larger company or higher EPS does not necessarily mean better allocation.
compare: Buyback prices and net share count
capital-allocation.watch: Buybacks can destroy value when shares are overpriced or liquidity is needed. Acquisition growth can conceal poor returns.
capital-allocation.where: Cash flow statement, acquisition notes, shareholder letters, and proxy disclosures.

value-trap.title: Value Trap
value-trap.short: An apparent bargain whose economics undermine the valuation thesis.
value-trap.what: A stock can look cheap on past profits or recorded assets while earning power, asset recoverability, or shareholder value deteriorates. The apparent discount may never have represented true value.
example: Sustainable EPS estimate after customer losses
value-trap.interp: Investigate why the price is low. Separate temporary setbacks from lasting damage, and identify evidence that would disprove your recovery assumptions.
value-trap.watch: A missing catalyst or a long period of undervaluation alone does not establish a value trap. A catalyst also cannot repair weak economics by itself.
value-trap.where: Multi-year statements, competitive evidence, and your thesis review.

incremental-roic.title: Incremental ROIC
incremental-roic.short: The additional operating profit earned on additional invested capital.
incremental-roic.what: Estimate how effectively a business turns new investment into additional after-tax operating profit. Use periods long enough for the investment to produce results.
incremental-roic.formula: Incremental ROIC ≈ Change in NOPAT / Change in Invested Capital
incremental-roic.interp: Compare incremental returns with the cost of capital. High returns on old assets do not prove new projects will earn similar returns.
better: Use consistent definitions and a sensible investment lag.
incremental-roic.watch: Acquisitions, inflation, timing, and write-downs distort the calculation. A near-zero or negative capital change makes the ratio hard to interpret.

reverse-dcf.title: Reverse DCF
reverse-dcf.short: Find the operating assumptions that reproduce the current market value.
reverse-dcf.what: Start with market value and solve for an assumption, such as revenue growth, that makes the discounted cash flows match it. Hold other assumptions explicit.
example: 7% fits this particular set of other assumptions
reverse-dcf.interp: Ask whether the required growth, margins, and reinvestment are plausible. Repeat with different discount rates and terminal assumptions. Test required Revenue Growth, Operating Margin and Free Cash Flow while explicitly fixing Terminal Growth, reinvestment and ROIC assumptions. Change one assumption at a time; many combinations can support the same value.
reverse-dcf.watch: Many combinations can explain one price. The implied growth rate is conditional, not an observable market forecast.
reverse-dcf.where: Your DCF model and current market capitalization, debt, and cash.
reverse-dcf.body:
Traditional DCF: Assumptions → Estimated Fair Value

Reverse DCF: Current Market Value → Required Future Performance
