interest-coverage.title: Interest Coverage
interest-coverage.short: Operating earnings relative to interest expense.
interest-coverage.what: A common measure compares EBIT with interest expense to assess the earnings available to cover financing costs.
interest-coverage.interp: Test coverage under weaker earnings and higher borrowing costs. This ratio does not show whether the principal can be repaid.
better: Adequate coverage depends on earnings stability and financing terms.
interest-coverage.watch: Zero interest expense makes this ratio undefined. Negative EBIT indicates earnings do not cover interest. EBITDA-based coverage is a different measure.

refinancing-risk.title: Refinancing Risk
refinancing-risk.short: The risk that maturing debt cannot be replaced on workable terms.
refinancing-risk.what: A company may need a new loan or bond issue when existing debt matures. New funding may be unavailable, more expensive, or subject to tighter conditions.
refinancing-risk.interp: Map maturities against available liquidity, realistic cash generation, and committed credit facilities. Examine covenants and collateral.
refinancing-risk.watch: Undrawn facilities can have conditions. Restricted cash and optimistic asset-sale proceeds may not be available when needed.
refinancing-risk.where: Debt footnotes, liquidity disclosures, and credit agreements.

earnings-quality.title: Earnings Quality
earnings-quality.short: How faithfully reported earnings represent repeatable business performance.
earnings-quality.what: Assess whether profits depend on sustainable operations or on temporary events, estimates, and aggressive accounting. Reconcile profit with cash generation over time.
example: Are collection times increasing, or did sales timing and terms change?
earnings-quality.interp: Look for evidence in revenue recognition, capitalization policies, reserves, and repeated adjustments. A warning signal starts an investigation; it is not proof of misconduct.
earnings-quality.watch: High operating cash flow can come from delayed supplier payments or customer prepayments. Cash conversion alone does not establish earnings quality.
earnings-quality.where: Accounting policies, financial statements, and reconciliation notes.

fcff.title: Free Cash Flow to the Firm
fcff.short: Cash after operating reinvestment, before financing cash flows.
fcff.what: Cash available to debt and equity providers together. An operating approach starts with after-tax operating profit and deducts reinvestment.
fcff.formula: FCFF = EBIT × (1 − Tax Rate) + D&A − CapEx − Increase in Non-cash Operating Working Capital
fcff.interp: Discount FCFF at WACC to estimate operating business value. Then account for cash, debt, and other non-operating assets or claims to reach equity value.
better: Reinvestment can reduce current cash flow while supporting future returns.
fcff.watch: Reported OCF minus CapEx is not automatically FCFF because interest treatment can differ. This simplified formula assumes no other adjustments.

fcfe.title: Free Cash Flow to Equity
fcfe.short: Cash available to equity holders after reinvestment and net debt flows.
fcfe.what: Start with earnings after interest and taxes, adjust for reinvestment, and include borrowing less principal repayments.
fcfe.formula: FCFE = Net Income + D&A − CapEx − Increase in Non-cash Operating Working Capital + Net Borrowing
fcfe.interp: Discount FCFE at the cost of equity to value the equity claim directly. Do not subtract debt again from that equity valuation.
better: Extra borrowing can increase current FCFE without improving operations.
fcfe.watch: Match cash flows and discount rates. Adjust separately for omitted non-operating assets and other claims; avoid counting them twice.
fcfe.where: Equity cash-flow forecasts and financing schedules.

circle-of-competence.title: Circle of Competence
circle-of-competence.short: The businesses and risks you can evaluate with sufficient understanding.
circle-of-competence.what: Define where you understand how a business earns money, what can damage it, and which assumptions you can assess. Recognize the limits of that knowledge.
example: Research the gap or decline to value the opportunity
circle-of-competence.interp: Write down what you know, what you infer, and what you cannot assess. Expand your knowledge through evidence rather than familiarity alone.
circle-of-competence.watch: Using a product or knowing an industry’s vocabulary does not establish valuation competence.
circle-of-competence.where: Your research notes and decision checklist.

permanent-capital-loss.title: Permanent Capital Loss
permanent-capital-loss.short: An enduring loss of investment value, distinct from a temporary price fluctuation.
permanent-capital-loss.what: Business failure, lasting economic damage, severe dilution, or paying too much can leave an investment unable to recover its original purchasing power.
example: Price falls while well-supported earning power remains intact
Debt restructuring leaves shareholders with little ownership
permanent-capital-loss.interp: Analyze how the investment could fail economically. A share-price decline may signal that risk, but does not by itself prove permanent damage.
permanent-capital-loss.watch: Low price volatility does not establish safety. Forced selling can turn a temporary decline into a realized loss.
permanent-capital-loss.where: Scenario analysis and portfolio liquidity planning.

opportunity-cost.title: Opportunity Cost
opportunity-cost.short: The benefit forgone by choosing one use of capital over another.
opportunity-cost.what: Compare an investment with realistic alternatives, including retaining liquidity. Consider risk, time, taxes, and confidence in the estimates. Capital invested in one company cannot simultaneously be invested elsewhere. The opportunity cost of capital reflects alternatives with comparable risk.
example: Estimated 8% annual return with high uncertainty
The higher forecast alone does not settle the choice
$100 in five years has a PV of about $68.06 at 8%. Evaluate the delayed payment against that alternative.
opportunity-cost.interp: An investment can appear undervalued yet be less attractive than another available use of funds.
opportunity-cost.watch: Forecast precision is limited. Switching also has transaction costs and possible taxes.
opportunity-cost.where: Your investment comparisons and management allocation decisions.

management-incentives.title: Management Incentives
management-incentives.short: How compensation, ownership, and control influence management decisions.
management-incentives.what: Examine what managers are rewarded for and whether those rewards support lasting per-share value. Review targets, vesting periods, ownership, and governance.
example: Acquisitions increase revenue despite weak investment returns
management-incentives.interp: Compare stated priorities with actual pay formulas and capital allocation. Consider minority shareholders as well as controlling owners.
better: Alignment depends on incentive design and behavior.
management-incentives.watch: Large insider ownership can align interests but can also entrench control. Adjusted performance metrics may exclude real costs.
management-incentives.where: Proxy statements, remuneration reports, and ownership disclosures.

tangible-book-value.title: Tangible Book Value
tangible-book-value.short: Accounting equity after deducting goodwill and other intangible assets.
tangible-book-value.what: A balance-sheet measure that removes recorded goodwill and other intangibles from equity. For a common-share measure, also exclude preferred equity.
tangible-book-value.formula: Common Tangible Book Value = Total Equity − Preferred Equity − Goodwill − Other Intangible Assets
tangible-book-value.interp: This can help assess some asset-heavy businesses and financial institutions. It does not measure the full economic value of a franchise.
tangible-book-value.watch: Tangible book value is not liquidation value. Recorded assets may require write-downs, and liabilities or disposal costs may exceed expectations.
tangible-book-value.where: Balance sheet and goodwill, intangible-asset, and equity notes.

liquidation-value.title: Liquidation Value
liquidation-value.short: Estimated proceeds left for shareholders after assets are sold and claims are settled.
liquidation-value.what: Estimate realizable asset proceeds, then deduct liabilities, senior claims, and closure costs. Distinguish orderly sales from distressed sales.
liquidation-value.formula: Common Equity Liquidation Value ≈ Asset Sale Proceeds − Liabilities − Preferred Claims − Closure Costs
liquidation-value.interp: Use asset-specific recovery assumptions and allow for the time needed to sell assets. Investigate taxes, leases, pensions, and other obligations.
better: A large estimated surplus matters only if recoverable and accessible.
liquidation-value.watch: Book values are not sale prices. Operating losses can consume assets while shareholders wait, and closure costs are uncertain.
liquidation-value.where: Asset notes, claim schedules, appraisals, and wind-down estimates.

ncav.title: Net Current Asset Value
ncav.short: Current assets less all liabilities and claims senior to common equity.
ncav.what: A conservative asset-screening measure that excludes long-term assets but deducts all liabilities. A stock below this measure is often called a net-net candidate.
ncav.formula: Common NCAV = Current Assets − Total Liabilities − Preferred Equity
ncav.interp: Compare the measure with market capitalization, then examine asset recoverability and cash consumption. It is a research screen, not a purchase rule.
ncav.watch: Subtract all liabilities, not only current liabilities. NCAV can disappear through losses, poor allocation, or unrecoverable assets.

price-sales.title: Price-to-Sales
price-sales.what: Equity market value per dollar of revenue. Useful when earnings are negative or temporarily depressed.
price-sales.interp: Compare the same revenue period and similar businesses. Two companies with identical P/S can deserve very different valuations because margins, reinvestment and risk differ.
price-sales.watch: Does not account for debt or tell you whether sales are profitable. A low multiple is not proof of cheapness.
price-sales.short: Equity market value per dollar of revenue. Useful when earnings are negative or temporarily depressed.

ev-revenue.title: EV / Revenue
ev-revenue.what: Operating business value per dollar of revenue. Includes the cash/debt bridge, making comparisons across capital structures more useful than P/S alone.
ev-revenue.interp: Use consistent revenue periods. Consider Revenue Growth, Gross Margin, Operating Margin, expected future margins, capital intensity, Free Cash Flow potential, ROIC, competitive advantage and risk.
ev-revenue.watch: A multiple is not a valuation by itself. A high multiple does not automatically mean expensive; a low multiple does not automatically mean cheap.
ev-revenue.short: Operating business value per dollar of revenue. Includes the cash/debt bridge, making comparisons across capital structures more useful than P/S alone.
ev-revenue.body: A multiple is not a valuation by itself.

profitable-growth.title: Profitable Growth
profitable-growth.what: Revenue Growth measures expansion in sales; Profitable Growth asks whether that expansion creates economic value.
profitable-growth.interp: Ask: Is Revenue growing? Is Gross Margin stable or improving? Is Operating Margin improving? Is Free Cash Flow improving? Is ROIC improving?
profitable-growth.watch: Growth alone does not create shareholder value if it permanently destroys capital. Improving ROIC is not sufficient if returns remain below the cost of capital.
example: Sales +40%; return on new capital 4%; cost of capital 10%
Growth can destroy value despite higher revenue.
profitable-growth.short: Revenue Growth measures expansion in sales; Profitable Growth asks whether that expansion creates economic value.
profitable-growth.body:
Growth does not automatically create shareholder value.

Growth + ROIC > WACC → Potential value creation.

Growth + ROIC < WACC → Potential value destruction.

For new growth, test incremental ROIC: rapid Revenue Growth can destroy value when new investment earns less than its Cost of Capital.

operating-margin-trend.title: Operating Margin Trend
operating-margin-trend.what: The direction and durability of operating profitability across periods, not just today’s margin.
operating-margin-trend.interp: Compare quarter-over-quarter, year-over-year and multi-year trends. This reveals whether an early-stage or high-growth company is approaching a sustainable profit model.
operating-margin-trend.watch: Control for seasonality, acquisitions, one-off costs and accounting changes. An improving loss is progress, not proof of future profitability.
operating-margin-trend.body:
1. Operating Loss
  2. Smaller Operating Loss
  3. Operating Breakeven
  4. Positive Operating Margin
  5. Operating Margin Expansion
operating-margin-trend.short: The direction and durability of operating profitability across periods, not just today’s margin.

backlog.title: Backlog
backlog.what: Contracted future business that has not yet been recognized as Revenue. Reported definitions vary by company.
backlog.interp: Examine backlog growth, expected recognition period, cancellation risk, customer concentration, contract profitability and conversion into Revenue.
backlog.watch: Backlog ≠ Revenue. Backlog ≠ Profit. Backlog ≠ Cash Flow. Options, funding conditions and cancellations can change reported totals.
backlog.short: Contracted future business that has not yet been recognized as Revenue. Reported definitions vary by company.

backlog-quality.title: Backlog Quality
backlog-quality.what: The likelihood that contracted business converts into profitable revenue and collectible cash.
backlog-quality.interp: A large backlog is valuable only if the company can fulfill it profitably. Favor credible customers, realistic delivery schedules and sustainable contract margins.
backlog-quality.watch: Size alone hides cancellation rights, concentration, fixed-price cost overruns and execution constraints.
example: Large sales visibility, expected contract loss.
backlog-quality.short: The likelihood that contracted business converts into profitable revenue and collectible cash.

deferred-revenue.title: Deferred Revenue
deferred-revenue.what: A contract liability generally arising when payment is received, or becomes due, before the related goods or services are transferred.
deferred-revenue.interp: Customer prepayments can finance operations. Unlike Backlog, Deferred Revenue reflects advance consideration received or due for unfulfilled performance; definitions and overlap must be checked in the notes.
deferred-revenue.watch: Billing is not necessarily cash collection. Do not add Deferred Revenue to Backlog if it is already included in the reported Backlog.
example: After one month: revenue / remaining liability
deferred-revenue.body:
Illustrative prepaid service:

  1. Customer pays
  2. Cash received
  3. Deferred Revenue liability
  4. Product/service delivered
  5. Revenue recognized
deferred-revenue.short: A contract liability generally arising when payment is received, or becomes due, before the related goods or services are transferred.

contracted-sales.title: Contracted Sales
contracted-sales.what: Sales value announced under signed agreements, often covering several future periods. It is not a standardized substitute for recognized revenue.
contracted-sales.interp: Read contract duration, enforceability, cancellation clauses, delivery obligations and collection terms. Distinguish each stage in the comparison below.
contracted-sales.watch: A press release announcing billions in signed contracts does not mean billions in Revenue were generated during that period. Do not sum overlapping contract metrics.
contracted-sales.body:
Contracted SalesSigned agreement value; may span years.
BacklogContracted business not yet recognized as Revenue.
Deferred RevenueAdvance consideration received or due before performance.
Recognized RevenueGoods/services transferred under accounting rules.
Cash ReceivedActual collection; can precede or follow recognition.
contracted-sales.short: Sales value announced under signed agreements, often covering several future periods. It is not a standardized substitute for recognized revenue.

revenue-recognition.title: Revenue Recognition
revenue-recognition.what: Revenue is recorded as promised goods or services are transferred to the customer—at a point in time or over time as performance obligations are satisfied.
revenue-recognition.interp: An order signals demand; a contract sets obligations; cash collection records payment. Recognition follows delivery/performance under the accounting rules, not simply the signature or payment date.
revenue-recognition.watch: Orders can be cancelled and cash can arrive before or after Revenue. Use accounting policies and contract notes to understand timing.
example: Equipment delivered in March, paid in April
Revenue may be recognized in March; cash arrives in April.
revenue-recognition.short: Revenue is recorded as promised goods or services are transferred to the customer—at a point in time or over time as performance obligations are satisfied.

capex-efficiency.title: CapEx Efficiency
capex-efficiency.what: How effectively capital spending produces future economic returns. Falling CapEx is not automatically good; rising CapEx is not automatically bad.
capex-efficiency.interp: What economic return is the company generating from incremental capital investment? Connect spending to capacity, Revenue, Operating Leverage, Free Cash Flow and ROIC.
capex-efficiency.watch: Compare investment cohorts over appropriate lags. The examples are signals to investigate, not causal proof. Falling spending can reflect underinvestment; high growth can require substantial reinvestment.
capex-efficiency.short: How effectively capital spending produces future economic returns. Falling CapEx is not automatically good; rising CapEx is not automatically bad.

embedded-expectations.title: Embedded Expectations
embedded-expectations.what: Today’s stock price already reflects expectations about future performance.
embedded-expectations.interp: What must happen for today’s valuation to make sense? Test Revenue Growth, future Operating Margin, Free Cash Flow Margin, ROIC, market share, Total Addressable Market and the duration of high growth.
embedded-expectations.watch: A great company can still be a poor investment if the market price assumes an unrealistically successful future. Price alone cannot uniquely identify all implied assumptions.
example: Price requires 30% growth for ten years
Test market size, competition and funding needs before accepting it.
embedded-expectations.short: Today’s stock price already reflects expectations about future performance.
